n: Jesus enters Jericho, the last major stop on His journey before the climb to Jerusalem.

f.g: A prosperous city on a major trade route — a natural place for a tax office.

n: Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector — a supervisor over other tax collectors — and he is wealthy, likely from overcharging people. Ironically, his name means “pure” or “innocent.”

f.g: From the Hebrew Zakkai, “pure, righteous.”
A head tax collector, the only time this title appears in the New Testament.

n: He wants to see who Jesus is, but he is short and can’t see over the crowd — a crowd that may not have been eager to make room for him.

f.g: Crowd.
Short.

n: Forgetting his dignity, he runs ahead and climbs a tree along the route. Wealthy men didn’t usually run or climb trees — his desire outweighs his pride.

f.g: A sycamore-fig, with low, spreading branches easy to climb — not the same as an American sycamore.

n: Jesus stops, looks up, and calls him by name, inviting Himself to stay at his house today. Zacchaeus was seeking Jesus, but Jesus was seeking him.

f.g: Jesus knows his name before they are introduced.
Stay.

n: Zacchaeus hurries down and welcomes Jesus with joy. Being known and wanted by Jesus changes him.
The crowd grumbles that Jesus is going to be the guest of a notorious sinner. To eat with someone was to accept him.

f.g: Grumbled.

n: Zacchaeus stands and makes a public commitment: half his wealth to the poor, and fourfold repayment to anyone he cheated — far more than the law required. This is repentance in action.

f.g: The law of Moses required fourfold restitution only for certain thefts; usually it was the amount plus one-fifth.
Extortion — demanding more than was owed.

n: Jesus declares that salvation has come to this household. Despised as he was, Zacchaeus is a true son of Abraham, an heir of the covenant.
This verse sums up Jesus’ entire mission: He came to seek out and save the lost.

f.w: to seek and to save that which was lost

n: Near Jerusalem, many expect God’s kingdom to appear immediately in political triumph. Jesus tells a parable to correct that expectation: there will be a delay.

f.g: They expected Jesus to establish His kingdom on arrival in Jerusalem.

n: A nobleman travels to a distant land to be appointed king, then plans to return. Jesus would go to heaven and return later in glory. Listeners might also recall Archelaus, a son of Herod who went to Rome seeking kingship.

f.g: Historically, Herod’s sons went to Rome to have their rule confirmed by Caesar.

n: Before leaving, he gives each of ten servants one pound and tells them to do business with it until he returns. Each receives the same trust.

f.g: Greek mna (mina), about 100 days’ wages.
Do business, put it to work.

n: But his citizens hate him and send word that they don’t want him as king. Some reject Christ’s rule outright.

f.w: We will not have this man to reign over us

n: Having been crowned, he returns and calls in his servants to see what each gained. Christ will return and ask for an accounting.
The first servant has multiplied the money tenfold.

f.g: He humbly credits the master’s money, not himself.

n: The master praises him: faithful in a very small thing, he now receives authority over ten cities. Faithfulness is rewarded far out of proportion.
The second servant has made five pounds.

f.g: A good result, though less than the first.

n: He receives five cities. Reward matches faithfulness.

f.g: Responsibility grows according to diligence.

n: Another servant returns the original pound, which he has kept wrapped in a cloth. He did nothing with it.

f.g: A cloth, such as a sweat cloth or handkerchief.

n: He blames his master, calling him harsh and demanding. Fear and a false view of the master paralyzed him.

f.g: Strict, harsh, severe.

n: The master judges him by his own words: if you believed I was so demanding, you should have acted accordingly.

f.w: Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee

n: He could at least have deposited the money with bankers to earn interest. Doing nothing was the real failure.

f.g: Interest (not necessarily excessive, as the modern word implies).

n: The master orders the pound taken from him and given to the servant who has ten.
Bystanders object: but he already has ten! It seems unfair.

f.g: A parenthetical protest from the listeners.

n: Those who use what they have receive more; those who neglect their gifts lose them. Spiritual gifts grow through use.

f.w: unto every one which hath shall be given

n: The enemies who rejected the king’s rule face judgment. The parable ends with a sober warning that rejecting Christ has consequences.

f.g: Ancient kings dealt harshly with rebels; the image depicts final judgment.

n: Having finished speaking, Jesus leads the way up the steep road to Jerusalem — determined, walking ahead of His disciples.

f.g: From Jericho the road climbs about 3,500 feet in roughly 17 miles.

n: Approaching villages on the Mount of Olives just east of Jerusalem, He sends two disciples ahead.

f.g: Villages on the eastern slopes of the Mount of Olives; Bethany was home to Mary, Martha, and Lazarus.

n: They will find a colt that no one has ever ridden. An animal never used for ordinary work was considered fit for sacred purposes.

f.g: A young donkey (Matthew and John specify a donkey).

n: If anyone asks, they are to say that the Lord needs it. Jesus knows what they will encounter.

f.w: the Lord hath need of him
f.g: “Lord” here may mean Jesus, or the owner may have been a disciple who would understand.

n: They go and find everything exactly as He said.

f.w: found even as he had said

n: As they untie the colt, its owners ask what they are doing.

f.g: Untying.

n: They give the answer Jesus told them, and the owners allow it.

f.w: The Lord hath need of him
f.g: Obedience to precise instructions brings the expected result.

n: They throw their cloaks on the colt as a saddle and help Jesus mount. Riding a donkey fulfilled Zechariah’s prophecy of a humble, peaceful king.
People spread their cloaks on the road before Him, a royal welcome like that given to Israel’s ancient kings.

f.w: spread their clothes in the way

n: As the road descends the Mount of Olives with Jerusalem in full view, His disciples burst into loud praise for all the miracles they have seen.

f.w: the descent of the mount of Olives
f.g: From here the whole city and temple would come suddenly into view.

n: They hail Him as King, quoting Psalm 118. Their “peace in heaven” echoes the angels’ song at His birth.

f.w: Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord

n: Some Pharisees, alarmed at the royal claims, tell Jesus to silence His followers.

f.g: Messianic claims could provoke Roman retaliation.

n: Jesus answers that if they were silent, the very stones would cry out. Creation itself must acknowledge its King.

f.w: the stones would immediately cry out

n: Coming near, Jesus sees the city and weeps over it — sobbing aloud. Amid the cheering, He grieves for those who will reject Him.

f.g: A word meaning to weep aloud, to lament.

n: If only Jerusalem had recognized, on this day of all days, what would bring it peace! But now it is hidden from them. There is a play on words: Jerusalem means “foundation of peace.”

f.w: the things which belong unto thy peace

n: He foresees enemy armies building siege works around the city and surrounding it on all sides. The Romans did exactly this in AD 70.

f.g: Build a siege rampart or palisade.
Surround you.

n: They will flatten the city and its people, leaving not one stone on another — because Jerusalem did not recognize the time when God came to visit and save it.

f.g: The time when God came in person to bless and redeem them.

f.w: not leave in thee one stone upon another

n: Jesus enters the temple and begins driving out the merchants. Selling animals and exchanging money had turned the Court of the Gentiles into a marketplace.

f.g: Merchants selling sacrificial animals, often at inflated prices.

n: He quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: God’s house should be a house of prayer, but they have turned it into a hideout for robbers.

f.w: My house is the house of prayer

n: He teaches in the temple every day. Meanwhile the chief priests, scribes, and leading men look for a way to kill Him.

f.g: Leading citizens, probably elders of the Sanhedrin council.

n: They can’t find a way, because the people hang on His every word. His popularity protects Him — for now.

f.g: Literally “hung upon him, listening.”
